payload.native_system_prompt:
You are part of an optimization system that improves a given text (i.e. the variable). You are the gradient (feedback) engine. Your only responsibility is to give intelligent and creative feedback and constructive criticism to variables, given an objective specified in <OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> </OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> tags. The variables may be solutions to problems, prompts to language models, code, or any other text-based variable. Pay attention to the role description of the variable, and the context in which it is used. You should assume that the variable will be used in a similar context in the future. Only provide strategies, explanations, and methods to change in the variable. DO NOT propose a new version of the variable, that will be the job of the optimizer. Your only job is to send feedback and criticism (compute 'gradients'). For instance, feedback can be in the form of 'Since language models have the X failure mode...', 'Adding X can fix this error because...', 'Removing X can improve the objective function because...', 'Changing X to Y would fix the mistake ...', that gets at the downstream objective.
If a variable is already working well (e.g. the objective function is perfect, an evaluation shows the response is accurate), you should not give feedback.

### Glossary of tags that will be sent to you:
# - <LM_SYSTEM_PROMPT>: The system prompt for the language model.
# - <LM_INPUT>: The input to the language model.
# - <LM_OUTPUT>: The output of the language model.
# - <OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION>: The objective of the optimization task.
# - <VARIABLE>: Specifies the span of the variable.
# - <ROLE>: The role description of the variable.
payload.instruction: Make her close her jacket fully
payload.rubric: Judge requested image editing: yes means all requested changes are complete, no means no requested change has progressed, partial means some progress without complete fulfillment. Unrelated edits are not requested progress. Insufficient evidence stays unresolved.

node.question: Is the woman's jacket fully closed in the edited image?
node.criteria: Pass only if the jacket's front panels meet across the closure and no visible opening remains. Fail if a visible opening remains. Unknown if the front closure cannot be seen well enough to determine whether the panels meet; do not infer closure or an opening from pose, viewpoint, or fabric motion alone.
node.binding: Identify the woman's jacket in the edited image and inspect its front closure directly. Use the source image only to identify the same jacket and provide context; assess complete closure in the edited image, not change in pose or garment motion.

node_traces.evidence: The woman's jacket is visible in the edited image, and its front panels are separated with a clear opening; they do not meet across the closure.

d1-progress: The binding already targets the right partial-progress criterion, but the trace shows a high-confidence unknown because the edited pose and flaring obscure a direct comparison. Make the decision procedure explicitly seek comparable visual evidence of the same jacket’s front opening across both images, accounting for pose and viewpoint changes (for example, compare visible panel edges and opening width only where both are discernible). Do not infer progress from the turn or flare alone. If the panels remain unassessable, preserve unknown rather than forcing yes/no; confidence or the reference label is not evidence. This is a visual-evidence limitation, not a transport, schema, or dependency failure. The reference label constrains aggregate evaluation but does not establish that this particular partial-progress check is positive; keep partial progress distinct from the instruction’s full-closure requirement.

response.content: {"text":"The node already asks the right full-closure question, and its trace is valid, queried, and dependency-free; this is not a transport or schema failure. The edited image shows the woman turned sideways with the jacket flaring, so the trace’s claim of a clear front opening is not well supported by a direct view of the closure. Refine the binding/criterion to require inspecting the same jacket’s front closure in the edited image and to distinguish a genuinely visible gap from fabric displaced by pose or motion. Use the source only to identify the garment, not to infer edited closure. If the closure cannot be assessed directly, return unknown rather than treating the flare as proof of an opening or forcing a label. The reference label is aggregate guidance, not atomic ground truth; do not change the criterion merely to match it. Keep this complete-closure check distinct from any partial-progress check."}
